title: Radioactivity and Nuclear Decay Laws
short_intro: Radioactivity is the spontaneous disintegration of unstable atomic nuclei accompanied by the emission of ionizing radiation such as alpha particles, beta particles, and gamma rays. The process follows a statistical first-order decay law independent of external physical and chemical conditions.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Basic properties of alpha, beta, and gamma rays, radioactive displacement laws, half-life, mean life, and simple radioactive decay law.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Successive transformations, radioactive equilibrium, secular and transient equilibrium, carbon dating, alpha-decay tunneling theory, and neutrino hypothesis in beta decay.

concept_notes.heading: Nature and Properties of Radiations
bullets: Alpha particles are doubly ionized helium nuclei (42He) carrying a charge of +2e and a mass approximately four times that of a proton.
Beta particles are high-speed electrons (or positrons) originating from the nucleus via neutron-proton conversion.
Gamma rays are high-frequency electromagnetic quanta emitted during transitions between nuclear energy states.

concept_notes.heading: Law of Radioactive Decay
bullets: The rate of disintegration of radioactive nuclei is directly proportional to the number of undecayed nuclei present at that instant.
The decay probability per unit time is a constant characteristic of the radioactive species, known as the decay constant.
Radioactive decay is a purely statistical phenomenon; it is impossible to predict the exact moment a specific nucleus will decay.

concept_notes.heading: Half-Life and Mean Life
bullets: Half-life (T1/2) is the time interval required for the number of active nuclei to reduce to half of its initial value.
Mean life (τ) is the sum of the ages of all nuclei divided by the total number of nuclei initially present, representing the reciprocal of the decay constant.
Both parameters are independent of temperature, pressure, chemical combination, and initial quantity.

concept_notes.heading: Radioactive Equilibrium
bullets: In a chain of successive disintegrations (A → B → C), if the half-life of parent A is much greater than that of daughter B, secular equilibrium is established.
At secular equilibrium, the activity of the daughter nuclide equals the activity of the parent nuclide.
Transient equilibrium occurs when the parent's half-life is longer than the daughter's, but of comparable magnitude.

derivations.title: Exponential Decay Law
derivations.conditions: Single radioactive isotope with constant decay constant λ
steps: Write the differential rate equation: dN/dt = -λN
Integrate both sides from N0 at t = 0 to N at time t: ∫ (dN / N) = -λ ∫ dt

derivations.title: Relation between Half-Life and Decay Constant
steps: Substitute N = N0 / 2 and t = T1/2 into the decay equation
Cancel N0 and take natural logarithm of both sides: ln(2) = λ T1/2

formula_sheet.name: Decay Law Equation
formula_sheet.variables: N(t) = nuclei at time t, N_0 = initial nuclei, \lambda = decay constant
formula_sheet.conditions: Constant decay probability per unit time

formula_sheet.name: Nuclei Remaining after n Half-Lives
formula_sheet.variables: n = number of half-lives elapsed (t / T_{1/2})

formula_sheet.name: Secular Equilibrium Condition
formula_sheet.variables: \lambda_1, N_1 = parent decay constant and number; \lambda_2, N_2 = daughter parameters

formula_sheet.name: Successive Decay General Equation (Bateman Solution for Daughter)
formula_sheet.variables: N_2(t) = daughter nuclei, N_{10} = initial parent nuclei

formula_sheet.name: Alpha Decay Energy (Q-value)
formula_sheet.variables: m_p = parent mass, m_d = daughter mass, m_\alpha = alpha particle mass
formula_sheet.conditions: Conservation of relativistic energy and momentum

graphs_and_experiments.title: Exponential Decay Curve
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A rectangular hyperbola-like decreasing curve of N versus t, showing successive halving of N at equal time intervals T1/2.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Demonstrates that the number of radioactive nuclei decreases exponentially with time.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Used to graphically determine half-life and decay constant.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Logarithmic Decay Curve
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A straight line plot of ln(N) versus t with a negative slope equal to -λ and y-intercept ln(N0).
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Linearization of the exponential law allows precise calculation of the decay constant from experimental data.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Tested in numerical and conceptual questions regarding slope interpretation.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Geiger-Müller Counter Characteristic Curve
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Count rate versus applied potential difference showing the starting voltage, plateau region, and discharge region.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Identifies the working plateau where count rate is independent of voltage fluctuations.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Instrumental setup questions in practical-oriented physics examinations.

solved_numericals.question: The half-life of a radioactive substance is 4 days. If the initial mass is 64 g, find the mass remaining after 12 days.
solution_steps: Determine the number of half-lives elapsed: n = t / T_{1/2} = 12 / 4 = 3

solved_numericals.question: A radioactive material has a decay constant of 0.05 day<sup>-1</sup>. Calculate its mean life and the time taken for 75% of the sample to decay.
solution_steps: For 75% decay, the remaining fraction is 25%, i.e., N / N_0 = 0.25 = (1/2)^2, meaning 2 half-lives have passed.
Alternatively, use t = -(1 / λ) ln(N / N_0) = -(1 / 0.05) ln(0.25) = -20 * (-1.386) = 27.72 days
solved_numericals.answer: Mean life = 20 days, Time taken = 27.72 days

solved_numericals.question: In a radioactive series, nuclide A decays to B with a decay constant λ1 = 0.1 h-1, and B decays to stable C with λ2 = 0.5 h-1. Initially, only A is present with N10 = 1000 nuclei. Find the number of daughter nuclei B at t = 0.
solution_steps: Use the general equation for daughter nuclei B: N_2(t) = [(λ_1 N_{10}) / (λ_2 - λ_1)] [exp(-\lambda_1 t) - exp(-\lambda_2 t)]
Therefore, at t = 0, the number of daughter nuclei B is zero.

assumptions_and_limitations: Radioactivity is assumed to be an entirely nuclear property unaffected by external physical conditions such as temperature, pressure, or electric and magnetic fields. However, orbital electron capture decay rates can show extremely minute variations under extreme chemical environments.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Radioactivity rate decreases over time because radioactive atoms 'get old' or fatigue.
common_misconceptions.correct: The decay probability of an individual nucleus remains constant over time; the decrease in total activity is due to the decreasing number of remaining undecayed nuclei.
common_misconceptions.why: Radioactive decay is a random, memoryless Poisson process.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Gamma rays carry a net positive or negative electric charge.
common_misconceptions.correct: Gamma rays are uncharged electromagnetic photons.
common_misconceptions.why: Unlike alpha and beta particles, gamma rays are not deflected by electric or magnetic fields.
